title: The three jewels, now
hookLine: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha, as you know them after five years
tomorrow: why did the Buddha hold up a handful of leaves?

cards: Every shop has a first customer, and almost nobody remembers who it was. The Buddhist story remembers its first two by name.
Tapussa and Bhallika, merchants traveling a trade road, came upon the Buddha soon after his awakening and offered him food. Then they asked to become his followers. And here's the odd part.
They took refuge in two jewels, the Buddha and his teaching. Not three. There was no sangha yet.
No community to go to. Just two men on a road, and a teacher who had nobody yet.

teach.b: The sangha came after: the first monks, then more, and in the Vinaya a father searching for his missing son becomes the first lay follower to go for refuge to all three. Three jewels: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha.
Three places to rest. A refuge is a shelter you go to in a storm, not a fortress you never leave. You go in, and you come back out a little steadier.

teach.h: A WEEK, ONE DAY AT A TIME.
teach.b: Now hold up this week, one day at a time. The Kalamas, told to know for themselves: his own words. Assaji, the beginner with one verse: the great story.
The arahant and the bodhisattva: many doors. Thus have I heard: the sources. One arrow, not two: the first words.
Two kitchens, two verses: the verses stayed.

teach.h: THE JEWELS IN ALL OF IT.
teach.b: Look again and the jewels are in all of it. The Buddha, as someone who showed a way and handed back the test. The dhamma, as words you've heard, carried and tried.
The sangha, as the beginners, elders, grandparents and friends who passed it to you.
Five years on, the three may not look the way they did on the first day.
They're still three places to rest.

how: Buddhists go for refuge to the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, often by reciting the three refuges, three times over, at the start of a service, a retreat or a daily sit.

o: the Buddha, his teaching and the community: the three refuges
three sacred relics kept in the oldest Buddhist temples
three vows a monk takes on the day of his ordination

games.q: the week in jewels — tap the pairs.
p: showed a way, handed back the test
the people who passed it on

s: the first lay followers took refuge in all three jewels
Tapussa and Bhallika took refuge in two; the sangha didn't exist yet.
the refuges are traditionally recited three times
the Pali lines go round once, then a second time, then a third.

games.q: a friend moving across the country says, 'my practice is tied to my temple. once i leave, it's gone.' what do the three jewels say?
o: the jewels go with you: the Buddha's example, the dhamma you carry, and friends to find there.
she's right; refuge only works inside the building where you first took it.
only the Buddha matters; teaching and community are optional extras.
games.why: the first followers took refuge on a road, before there was even a sangha. the jewels are places to rest, not one address.

practice: Close your eyes. On three breaths, rest in each in turn: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha.
If you go for refuge, you can say the old Pali silently, Buddham saranam gacchami, I go for refuge to the Buddha, and on through the three. Then let the rest of the sit be just that, a place to rest.

wordCard.voice: The three jewels: the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, the three refuges. The first followers had two; you have all three.

orig.note: Pali: refuge, shelter; said in each of the three refuges.

carryVoice: Your line: three places to rest, wherever you are. A week of looking back, done.
